opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this is one of the key uncertainties right now. We've seen really dramatic progress on things like competitive programming and contest math, where models went from fairly weak to roughly top-human-competitor level over a pretty short period. A big part of why is that these are domains where you can do reinforcement learning really effectively. You have clean, verifiable feedback: the code passes the test cases or it doesn't, the answer is correct or it isn't. So you can just throw a lot of RL compute at it and get big gains.

The question is how much that transfers. I think there are a few different views. One view is that these skills are pretty narrow. Competitive programming problems are self-contained, short-horizon, and well-specified, and real-world work is messy. It involves long contexts, ambiguous goals, coordinating with other people, and judging whether something is actually good when there's no test suite telling you. On that view, you'll keep seeing amazing benchmark numbers that don't translate proportionally into, say, automating a software engineer's job.

My view is somewhere in the middle, maybe leaning toward more transfer than skeptics expect, but less than the most bullish people suggest. There's some real generalization. Models trained heavily with RL on math and code seem to get better at reasoning more broadly, at being careful, and at checking their work. And the bigger point is that the playbook generalizes, even if the specific skills don't fully transfer. If you can build RL environments for agentic software engineering tasks, which AI companies are clearly working hard on, you can probably get similar rapid progress there. The bottleneck shifts to how well you can construct good, scalable, hard-to-game training environments for messier tasks.

So the thing I'd watch is less "does a model that's good at contest math automatically become good at everything," and more "how quickly can labs extend this kind of verifiable-feedback training to longer-horizon, fuzzier tasks." Software engineering and AI research engineering are especially important here, because they're relatively checkable compared to many domains, and they're exactly the capabilities that matter most for AI accelerating its own development. If progress on those agentic tasks looks anything like what we saw in competitive programming, things could move quite fast. But there's real uncertainty, and I think it's plausible that the messier, longer-horizon parts turn out to be meaningfully harder and slow things down by a few years.

r002.rationale: It attributes rapid gains in competitive programming and contest math largely to effective reinforcement learning with clean, verifiable feedback.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is: it's complicated, and I want to separate a few things that often get lumped together.

The first thing to say is that competitive programming and competition maths are, in some sense, the easiest possible domains for current training methods. You have a crisp, verifiable reward signal — the code passes the tests or it doesn't, the proof is right or it isn't — and you can generate enormous amounts of synthetic practice. So it's not that surprising that these are the areas where we've seen the fastest progress. The question is how much that transfers to the stuff that actually matters economically, which is mostly long-horizon, messy, underspecified work where nobody hands you a test suite.

My view is that the transfer is real but incomplete. A lot of what makes a model good at hard competition problems — sustained reasoning, searching over approaches, noticing when something isn't working and backing off — does seem to generalise somewhat to things like agentic software engineering. You can see this in the fact that models that got dramatically better at maths also got better at, say, working through a large codebase for several hours. It wasn't a totally siloed capability.

But I'd push back on anyone who looks at, like, IMO gold and says "therefore AI is about to automate research." The gap between "can solve a very hard, cleanly posed problem in a few hours" and "can run a months-long project where you have to figure out what the problem even is, deal with ambiguity, manage your own context, and not go off the rails" — that gap is still pretty large. The things I'd actually watch are the horizon length metrics: how long a task can the model do autonomously, with reasonable reliability? That's been growing at something like doubling every several months, and if that continues, it eventually matters a lot. But the competitive programming benchmarks themselves are mostly saturated and I don't think they're that informative anymore.

The other thing I'd flag is that there's a question of how much of the progress is coming from RL on verifiable domains specifically, and whether that well runs dry. If most of the recent gains come from "we found domains where we can check the answer and we hammered on them," then you'd expect capabilities to be very jagged — superhuman on things with a verifier, surprisingly weak on things without one. And I think that's roughly what we see. The real test is whether labs can get the same kind of gains in domains where the feedback is noisy or slow — things like research taste, or whether an experiment was actually worth running.

So where I land: I'd put meaningful probability on the trend continuing and this stuff translating into something like automating a large chunk of AI research within, say, a handful of years. But I'd also put real probability on it stalling out in a way where we have models that are incredible at well-posed problems and still kind of mediocre as autonomous colleagues. And honestly, which of those worlds we're in matters enormously for how fast everything else goes.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s evidence that the systems are getting much better at some kinds of reasoning, but I wouldn’t expect a direct translation where reaching a particular competitive programming rating means you can now automate a particular fraction of software engineering.

Competitive programming has a pretty unusual structure: you get a clearly specified problem, you can test your answer, and success doesn’t require understanding a large existing codebase or figuring out what someone actually wants. Maths problems often have similar properties. Those are also properties that make these tasks particularly amenable to training with reinforcement learning, because you can check whether an answer is right.

So one question is how much of the progress is learning broadly useful strategies for reasoning, and how much is becoming very good at that particular kind of task. I’d expect some of both. You should update towards stronger broader capabilities, but there’s substantial uncertainty about how far the transfer goes.

For automating research or software engineering, I’d want to look at whether systems can sustain useful work over longer periods, notice when their approach isn’t working, and deal with problems where the success criterion is ambiguous. You can have a system that solves a very difficult, well-specified problem and still needs a lot of supervision on a project that a human would consider relatively routine.

That said, I wouldn’t assume those remaining limitations will take a long time to fix. If the underlying reasoning becomes strong enough, improving how systems use tools and organize their work could make a substantial difference. And they don’t have to automate the whole process to accelerate AI development: being very useful on some of the technical bottlenecks could already matter a lot.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s evidence that these systems can get quite good at tasks where you can check whether they succeeded. In competitive programming, you can run the code against tests. In maths, at least in some settings, you can check a proof. That gives you a way to train on problems that are substantially harder than the ones humans have explicitly demonstrated how to solve.

The big question is how far that transfers. Competitive programming involves a lot of reasoning, but it’s also a pretty particular activity. You get a clean problem statement, and you know what counts as success. A lot of useful work involves figuring out what the problem is, gathering information, and dealing with mistakes over a much longer period. So I wouldn’t take a strong contest result and directly translate it into, say, being able to do the job of a software engineer.

But I also wouldn’t be very reassured by that distinction. Software engineering has plenty of things you can check, and you can build training environments that look more like actual engineering work. And if the systems become useful for doing AI research, you don’t need equally strong progress across every economically valuable task for that to have very large implications.

So I’d update toward stronger broader capabilities, with substantial uncertainty about the timing. I’d especially watch whether they can reliably complete longer tasks in unfamiliar environments, rather than just whether their scores on these competitions keep going up.
